title.en: Wide-Column Databases: Cassandra

intro_text.en: Cassandra architecture/setup and cqlsh, keyspaces/tables/partitions, partition and clustering keys, typed CQL DDL/CRUD and WHERE/ORDER BY/LIMIT. Includes 14 real CQL programs and a verified synthetic CSV dataset for Practicals 4–6. nodetool/cluster health remains awareness only; the reference uses one physical node.

title.en: 3.1 Cassandra Foundations, Architecture and Keys

h.en: Cassandra Uses, Query-First Thinking and Peer Architecture

body.en:
Apache Cassandra is a distributed wide-column database suited to partition-oriented workloads such as sensor histories, application events and high-write-volume telemetry. CQL exposes typed tables; “wide-column” does not mean it is a columnar analytical warehouse.

Query first: write the required reads before choosing keys. “Latest readings for one device on one day” suggests a device/day partition and a time clustering column. Cassandra is not a drop-in SQL engine with arbitrary joins, subqueries and free sorting of every column.

Architecture, conceptually: peers own token ranges; a contacted node can coordinate an operation and communicate with replicas. There is no mandatory single write-primary for the whole Cassandra cluster. Partitioning decides data subsets; replication maintains additional copies. Replication/consistency settings affect guarantees—avoid a universal product-wide CP/AP slogan or a claim of perfect availability.

CO3: design and implement distributed datasets using Cassandra’s data model and CQL. Practicals 4–6 cover setup, query-shaped CRUD and an AI-related dataset.

Actual reference: real Cassandra 5.0.9, cqlsh 6.2.0, CQL 3.4.7, Python 3.13.16 and Temurin Java 17.0.21+9 on Debian 13 x86_64. Fourteen CQL scripts were executed on one private authenticated node. Logical partition results are real; multi-machine distribution, replication failover, production capacity and external hosting were not tested.

h.en: Keyspace → Table → Partition → Row → Typed Column

body.en:
A keyspace is a namespace for tables and defines options such as replication policy and durable writes. A table defines columns and a primary-key layout. A partition contains rows sharing the complete partition-key value.

LevelSensor-history example
KeyspaceOne disposable di04000031_u3_... lab namespace
Tablereadings_by_device_day
Partition(S01, 2026-10-29)
Row within partitionOne reading_at timestamp, such as 09:01 UTC
Regular columntemperature_c double; status text

Partitions are logical data units; a node may store many partitions and a partition may have replicas. The reference has four logical device/day partitions but only one physical node. Four partitions are not four machines or four copies.

Keyspaces/tables do not appear merely because a shell connects. Use explicit DDL, verify it with read-only system schema or DESCRIBE, and make an authorized stored-data round-trip. Do not modify system keyspaces.

h.en: Partition Key versus Clustering Columns: Parentheses Matter

body.en:
A complete primary key uniquely identifies a logical row. Its first component is the partition key; the remaining components are clustering columns. Extra parentheses make a multi-column composite partition key.

PRIMARY KEY (device_id, day, reading_at)
-- Partition key: device_id
-- Clustering columns: day, reading_at

PRIMARY KEY ((device_id, day), reading_at)
-- Composite partition key: device_id AND day together
-- Clustering column: reading_at

For PRIMARY KEY ((device_id,day),reading_at), both device and day must match to select the intended partition. Different days for S01 form different partitions; time orders rows inside each one. In PRIMARY KEY (device_id,day,reading_at), day is instead the first clustering column inside a device-only partition.

Growth matters: time bucketing bounds history only relative to the actual write rate and record size. Two readings/minute produce 2,880 readings/day; a much faster stream may need smaller buckets or another deliberate design. Estimate size, query load and skew—“one day” is not automatically safe at every rate.

Identity: two samples with exactly the same full key upsert the same row. If several events can share a millisecond timestamp, consider a justified tie-breaker and its query implications. SET cannot mutate the key into a new identity; key-layout changes require a new model/migration.

title.en: 3.2 Installation and cqlsh — Practical 4

h.en: Install a Compatible Private Server and Matching cqlsh

body.en:
1. Identify platform: follow the selected release’s official Linux/package/tarball instructions. On Windows, use an instructor-approved Linux/WSL2 or container environment rather than assuming a native Windows server install; only the Debian reference was tested here.
  2. Check prerequisites: Cassandra 5.0 documentation specifies Java 11 or 17; the reference deliberately uses patched Temurin 17.0.21+9, not an unrelated Java default. Use a Python version supported by the bundled cqlsh. The actual 5.0.9 client was verified with Python 3.13.16; do not assume older cqlsh packages support it.
  3. Obtain official binaries: download the selected release and verify its published checksum before extracting. The reference Apache 5.0.9 tarball was SHA-512 verified; its Java runtime archive was SHA-256 verified. These identify the tested run, not a timeless latest-release claim.
  4. Configure private access before starting: keep CQL, internode and management/JMX interfaces private; enable appropriate authentication/authorization. Do not expose factory defaults or an unauthenticated server publicly.
  5. Initialize authorized lab access: on a brand-new private instance, use the vendor’s administrative role procedure to create unique private credentials, verify the new login, then rotate/disable the factory role. The reference did so before any teaching scripts; no private password is shipped.
  6. Start and connect: use the service manager for your package, or a foreground process for a tarball. Record versions and verify a real authorized write/read, not only a client executable.
# Operating-system terminal, from the extracted release:
java -version
python3 --version
bin/cassandra -v
bin/cqlsh --version
# Private learning instance only: cassandra.yaml settings
listen_address: 127.0.0.1
rpc_address: 127.0.0.1
native_transport_port: 9043
authenticator: PasswordAuthenticator
authorizer: CassandraAuthorizer
# Keep internode and local JMX access private too.
# This is not a complete production/TLS configuration.
# Terminal A, after private settings and Java compatibility:
# Run from the extracted Cassandra distribution.
bin/cassandra -f
# A package installation may use the OS service manager.
# Do not start two servers against the same data directory.

Resource boundary: GTU recommends an 8 GB learning computer. The reference used a reduced 512 MiB Java heap for tiny synthetic fixtures in a constrained sandbox; this is not a production sizing or tuning recommendation. Binaries, database state and credentials stayed outside the project in an excluded private cache.

h.en: Connect with cqlsh and Create/Alter/Drop Keyspaces

body.en:
cqlsh is a client shell, not the database server. Use the client bundled with the chosen Cassandra release, because cross-version compatibility is not universally guaranteed. Enter a private password at a prompt or use a correctly permissioned private credentials file; never submit a password-bearing command, file or history.

# Terminal B: your own authorized private lab account.
bin/cqlsh 127.0.0.1 9043 -u YOUR_LAB_USER --disable-history
# Enter the password at the hidden prompt; never use -p SECRET.
# Default native CQL port is 9042; the reference uses 9043.
-- Inside cqlsh, not in the operating-system terminal:
SHOW VERSION;
SHOW HOST;
DESCRIBE KEYSPACES;
SELECT release_version, cql_version, data_center
FROM system.local WHERE key='local';

The authenticated reference SHOW VERSION reported cqlsh 6.2.0 | Cassandra 5.0.9 | CQL spec 3.4.7 | Native protocol v4. Native protocol version 4 was explicitly selected for this client run; it is not the Cassandra product version.

-- Fresh disposable lab namespace; never a production keyspace.
CREATE KEYSPACE di04000031_u3_manual
WITH replication = {'class':'NetworkTopologyStrategy',
                    'datacenter1':1};
USE di04000031_u3_manual;
ALTER KEYSPACE di04000031_u3_manual WITH durable_writes=true;
-- After your lab, drop ONLY the namespace you created:
-- USE system;
-- DROP KEYSPACE di04000031_u3_manual;

Replication map: NetworkTopologyStrategy refers to the actual datacenter name, verified as datacenter1 here. RF 1 fits the single-node lab and offers no extra replica for node loss. Do not copy a DC name or raise RF and pretend it creates machines/copies by itself. durable_writes=true retains commit-log use; this lab does not disable durability.

Shell versus CQL: SHOW, DESCRIBE, COPY and SOURCE are cqlsh commands; application drivers send native CQL statements. CQL uses semicolons, single-quoted string values and typed column definitions.

Safety: each full example creates a distinct di04000031_u3_ namespace. Use the supplied runner: it refuses a pre-existing name, marks ownership only after successful CREATE and drops only that captured namespace. A prefix alone is neither authorization nor a backup. If running manually, stop immediately after an unexpected CREATE/setup error—do not continue into an existing keyspace and its DROP footer.

title.en: 3.3 Typed CQL DDL and Safe Schema Changes

h.en: CREATE TABLE, Basic Types and UTC Values

body.en:
CQL is a typed language. Define column types and the primary key explicitly; a wrong int literal is not silently accepted as a different string identifier.

CREATE TABLE readings_by_device_day (
  device_id text, day date, reading_at timestamp,
  temperature_c double, status text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((device_id, day), reading_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (reading_at DESC);
-- Sample literals, not a complete INSERT statement:
int:       82
text:      'Asha'
boolean:   true
date:      '2026-10-29'
timestamp: '2026-10-29T09:00:00Z'
uuid:      11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111
text with apostrophe: 'Asha''s sensor'
TypePurpose / care
int / bigintSigned 32-bit / 64-bit integers; choose a suitable range.
textUTF-8 text; string values use single quotes.
timestampDate and time with millisecond precision; include an explicit zone.
dateCalendar date without a time-of-day component.
boolean / doubletrue/false and approximate binary fractional numeric data.
uuidAn identifier value; a UUID is not necessarily a time-sorting timeuuid.

Unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive/lowercased in normal CQL usage; double quotes name identifiers rather than ordinary string values. Escape a string apostrophe by doubling it. Primary-key components cannot be null.

The typed example stores a fixed UUID and UTC timestamp. Its JSON display converts dates/UUIDs to strings and timestamps to ISO UTC; these formatting choices do not change the stored CQL types. Use an appropriate exact numeric policy for money rather than assuming double is exact currency.

h.en: ALTER TABLE, New Null Values and DROP TABLE

body.en:
CREATE TABLE defines a new schema; ALTER TABLE ADD adds a regular column. Existing rows do not acquire invented default data: the example’s newly added city reads as null until it is written.

ALTER TABLE learner_schema ADD city text;
ALTER TABLE learner_schema WITH comment='Small schema-change lab';
ALTER TABLE learner_schema DROP city;
DROP TABLE learner_schema;
-- Requires the disposable table created in the full demo.
-- These are separate changes, not a primary-key migration.

The executable example creates its disposable table first, adds/writes/removes city, changes a comment and verifies schema metadata after DROP. A successful ALTER command is not proof that applications have migrated their data or validation rules.

Key limitation: do not treat ALTER as arbitrary repartitioning. Adding a primary-key component or changing a partition key is not an in-place data-model edit. Primary-key-column rename support changes a name, not which data is grouped together. Plan a new table and controlled migration when access requirements change.

Destruction: dropping a regular column removes that column’s data logically; dropping a table removes the table; dropping a keyspace removes all its contents. Do not experiment with these commands in system or real application namespaces, and do not assume they provide an undo action.

title.en: 3.4 CQL CRUD and Partition-Oriented Queries — Practical 5

h.en: INSERT and the Default Upsert Rule

body.en:
A normal Cassandra INSERT is an upsert: a new complete primary key creates a row; an existing key writes the specified regular columns. It does not normally throw a duplicate-key error, and it is not whole-row replacement.

-- Assumes the learners_by_id schema in the independent demo.
INSERT INTO learners_by_id (learner_id, name)
VALUES (1, 'Asha Patel');
-- Same key: supplied name changes; existing city/marks remain.

UPDATE learners_by_id SET name='Jai', marks=68
WHERE learner_id=99;
-- Missing key: normal UPDATE can create a row.

For learner 1, name becomes Asha Patel but existing Surat/82 remain. Inserting learner 4 with just a name creates a row with city/marks null. Repeating a complete row identity does not create another logical row with that key.

Conditional clauses such as IF NOT EXISTS/IF EXISTS use different lightweight-transaction semantics and have costs; they are not implicit in these basic operations. Ordinary writes do not return MongoDB-style matchedCount, modifiedCount or deletedCount, so query the intended state and handle errors deliberately.

h.en: SELECT Projection, WHERE Equality and Bounded IN

body.en:
SELECT retrieves the named columns. Use WHERE with the designed key rather than assuming every regular field can be filtered like SQL.

SELECT name, city FROM learners_by_id WHERE learner_id=2;
SELECT learner_id, name FROM learners_by_id
WHERE learner_id IN (1,3);
-- A missing key returns an empty result set, not a new row.

The fixture returns Ravi/Bharuch for ID 2, names for IDs 1 and 3, and no rows for 999. Selecting only needed columns reduces returned data; it does not modify storage or implement authorization.

IN on supported key positions can select multiple known values, but large lists may fan out to many partitions. Do not rely on IN result order as a global lexical/marks order. For composite partition keys, supply the intended values of every component; for multiple clustering columns, respect their left-to-right restrictions.

CQL is SQL-like but does not provide general joins/subqueries or unrestricted OR-style ad-hoc predicates. Use the documented CQL syntax and design another access table when the required read does not fit the key.

h.en: Inspect the Eight-Reading Fixture and Four Logical Partitions

body.en:
The synthetic sensor data is fixed, reproducible and not measured from live devices. The default time order within a partition is descending. Every independent sensor example includes its seed explicitly, except the CSV example, which actually imports its supplied file.

Device / dayUTC minute → temperature °C
S01 / 2026-10-2909:00 → 30.0; 09:01 → 31.0; 09:02 → 32.0
S02 / 2026-10-2909:00 → 28.0; 09:01 → 29.0
S01 / 2026-10-3009:00 → 33.0; 09:01 → 34.0
S03 / 2026-10-2909:00 → 27.0

The partition row counts are 3, 2, 2 and 1, totaling 8. SELECT DISTINCT device_id,day lists the four partition-key values, not four server addresses. Hash/token placement is not alphabetical ordering of the device IDs.

Observed versus inferred: the reference queries really retrieve the selected partitions, but they all reside on one physical local node with RF 1. This simulates partition-oriented dataset design; it is not an experiment proving distribution over a multi-node cluster.

h.en: WHERE Time Ranges, Clustering ORDER BY and LIMIT

body.en:
For a device/day partition, use the clustering timestamp to select a contiguous time interval. The table specifies reading_at DESC; the latest two readings are therefore 32.0 at 09:02 followed by 31.0 at 09:01.

SELECT reading_at, temperature_c FROM readings_by_device_day
WHERE device_id='S01' AND day='2026-10-29'
  AND reading_at >= '2026-10-29T09:00:00Z'
  AND reading_at <  '2026-10-29T09:02:00Z';

SELECT reading_at, temperature_c FROM readings_by_device_day
WHERE device_id='S01' AND day='2026-10-29'
ORDER BY reading_at ASC LIMIT 2;

The half-open interval [09:00,09:02) returns 31.0 and 30.0 in descending clustering order. Reversing to ASC with LIMIT 2 returns 30.0 then 31.0. Include a timezone; “09:00” without a zone can be ambiguous across machines.

ORDER BY is constrained: it uses permitted clustering order (or its supported reverse) with the required key restrictions. It is not “sort any field in any table.” With multiple clustering columns, their declared sequence matters.

LIMIT: controls returned row count; it does not build an index, fix an invalid WHERE or guarantee a fixed number of underlying reads. Avoid unbounded full-table reads merely because this eight-row fixture is small.

h.en: UPDATE, Missing Rows and the Correct Key Scope

body.en:
UPDATE learners_by_id SET city='Surat', marks=75
WHERE learner_id=2;
-- Read back; CQL does not return matchedCount/modifiedCount.
SELECT name, city, marks FROM learners_by_id WHERE learner_id=2;
-- marks=marks+5 is NOT ordinary int arithmetic in CQL.
-- Counter columns are a separate feature with restrictions.

The observed Ravi update reads back Surat/75. A separate UPDATE of missing learner 99 stores Jai/68 with city null: normal UPDATE can create data. Do not interpret success as proof that the row existed before the write.

For the shown regular-row updates, specify the intended complete row key. Static columns, counters and conditional writes have different rules and are not shortcuts for the simple schema. A primary-key value is row identity, not a mutable ordinary attribute.

Changing multiple tables or combining external actions is not automatically one SQL transaction. The examples are sequential and do not claim concurrency stress testing, payment integration or cross-node consistency experiments.

h.en: DELETE a Cell, a Row or a Selected Partition

body.en:
DELETE city FROM learners_by_id WHERE learner_id=1;
DELETE FROM learners_by_id WHERE learner_id=2;
DELETE FROM readings_by_device_day
WHERE device_id='S01' AND day='2026-10-29'
  AND reading_at='2026-10-29T09:02:00Z';
DELETE FROM readings_by_device_day
WHERE device_id='S02' AND day='2026-10-29';

These four statements have different scopes: delete Asha’s city cell; delete learner 2; delete one full-key S01 reading; delete all rows in the selected S02/day partition. In the reference, Asha retains name/82 with city null, learner 2 returns no rows, S01/day29 retains two readings, and S02/day29 retains zero.

Tombstones: logical deletion uses markers. Disappearance from SELECT is not proof of immediate physical disk erasure; physical cleanup depends on storage lifecycle and safe maintenance conditions. Do not teach repair/compaction procedures as part of this awareness-level unit.

Safety: check the keyspace and every key component. Read-back proves the selected fixture result, not that a pre-read count locked data against concurrent changes. The supplied ownership-aware runner cleans only its newly created lab namespace.

title.en: 3.5 Query-First Modeling, Filtering and CSV Input

h.en: One Access Pattern per Table and Denormalization Costs

body.en:
Start with two read requirements: (1) recent readings for one device/day, and (2) high-status readings for one day. The first uses readings_by_device_day; the second uses a separate readings_by_status_day table whose composite partition key is (status,day) and whose clustering columns are device_id then reading_at.

Deliberate duplication avoids a join or a broad scan for the shown reads. It also creates a consistency obligation: writes/corrections/deletions may need to update more than one representation.

Real demonstration: the high S01/day29 reading starts at 32.0 in both tables. Updating the base table makes it 35.0 there while the lookup table still reads 32.0. Only the explicit second write makes the lookup table read 35.0. These two updates are not automatically one cross-table SQL transaction.

No foreign-key constraint or cascade updates the second table for you. Define retry, correction and missing-data handling in a real application. The status labels here are synthetic input, not predictions from a trained AI model. Do not use a logged multi-partition batch as a universal bulk-loading or transaction shortcut.

h.en: Unsupported Filters, ALLOW FILTERING and Real Negative Cases

body.en:
Without a suitable index or access-table design, the demonstrated temperature-only query is rejected with InvalidRequest. The version with LIMIT 1 is also rejected; a small output limit does not legalize that query.

-- Expected rejection: no suitable index/query-first key here.
SELECT device_id, temperature_c FROM readings_by_device_day
WHERE temperature_c > 30.0 LIMIT 1;

-- Tiny fixture only: three rows in this selected partition.
SELECT reading_at, temperature_c FROM readings_by_device_day
WHERE device_id='S01' AND day='2026-10-29'
  AND temperature_c > 30.0 ALLOW FILTERING;

The allowed example fixes one known three-row partition and returns 32.0 and 31.0. ALLOW FILTERING permits residual work; it is not an index, a modeling repair or a latency promise. Prefer an appropriate query-first table or deliberately selected index when an access pattern must scale.

Additional real server rejections: a string where int is required; null primary key; ORDER BY an ordinary marks column; SET on the primary key; malformed SELECT syntax. Expected InvalidRequest/SyntaxException outcomes are captured from the server; the three valid rows remain unchanged.

Runner comments: @result labels display observed result sets; @expect marks an intentionally rejected statement. These are ordinary comments, not extra CQL syntax, and unexpected exceptions still fail the run. JSON preserves server result order rather than silently sorting on the client.

h.en: Import the AI/IoT Sensor CSV and Verify Stored Keys — Practical 6

body.en:
The companion sensors.csv contains eight synthetic, explicitly UTC readings in the same four logical partitions. COPY FROM is a cqlsh-only import command; it is not sent as native CQL through an application driver.

-- cqlsh-only command, from the folder with sensors.csv:
COPY readings_by_device_day
  (device_id, day, reading_at, temperature_c, status)
FROM 'sensors.csv' WITH HEADER=TRUE AND NUMPROCESSES=1
  AND DATETIMEFORMAT='%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z'
  AND MAXPARSEERRORS=0 AND MAXINSERTERRORS=0
  AND MINBATCHSIZE=1 AND MAXBATCHSIZE=1;
-- Verify stored row count AND timestamps, not just import progress.

Why check timestamps: date/time parsing or duplicate full primary keys can collapse distinct input records into upserts. A message saying eight rows were processed/imported is not enough. The tested program verifies eight stored rows, every stored reading against the CSV, four distinct device/day partitions and latest S01/day29 time 09:02 UTC with 32.0.

Explicit format: DATETIMEFORMAT with %z recognizes the CSV’s UTC Z suffix. Do not depend on a permissive date-only fallback or an unrelated system timezone. HEADER, column mapping and error limits are deliberate; the single worker is for a tiny reference, not an import-throughput recommendation.

Honest scope: this fixed snapshot simulates time-stamped AI/IoT input. It is not live sensor ingestion, a trained model, a production ETL job or a multi-machine distribution benchmark. COPY’s varying timing/rate text is omitted from published output; completion and subsequent server-read results are real.

title.en: 3.6 Simple Analytics, Health Awareness and Practical Evidence

h.en: Bounded Per-Partition Analytical Features, Not a Trained Model

body.en:
Counts, totals, means and extrema can summarize a small sensor/day history for a report or later model input. Query the intended bounded partition rather than assuming Cassandra is an unrestricted analytical warehouse.

SELECT count(*) AS samples, sum(temperature_c) AS total,
  avg(temperature_c) AS mean, min(temperature_c) AS minimum,
  max(temperature_c) AS maximum
FROM readings_by_device_day
WHERE device_id='S01' AND day='2026-10-29';
Selected partitionObserved summary
S01 / 29 October3 samples; total 93.0; mean 31.0; min 30.0; max 32.0
S02 / 29 October2 samples; mean 28.5
S01 / 30 October2 samples; mean 33.5
S03 / 29 October1 sample; mean 27.0

Calculation: (30+31+32)/3 = 31; (28+29)/2 = 28.5. These are simple measured-feature calculations on the synthetic fixture. A mean/threshold flag is not a trained anomaly detector or a guaranteed real-time decision system.

For real analytics, consider data volume, query frequency, retention, partition growth and suitable downstream tools. Small full-table COUNT queries used only to verify the eight-row import are not advice to scan a production cluster for every request.

h.en: nodetool Awareness, Cluster Health and the Practical 4–6 Journal

body.en:
Scope: the syllabus requests a conceptual overview of cluster health and nodetool, at awareness level only. nodetool is a management tool that uses JMX, not a CQL query typed into cqlsh.

# OS terminal; read-only awareness, not a repair procedure:
bin/nodetool -h 127.0.0.1 -p 7199 status
# U = Up, D = Down
# N = Normal, L = Leaving, J = Joining, M = Moving
# Reference observation: one UN local node.
# UUID/load/ownership figures are environment-dependent.

Actual observation: a read-only nodetool status command reported one local UN node in datacenter1. U means Up and N means Normal. DN would describe Down/Normal; Joining/Leaving/Moving are other states to interpret, not instructions to trigger them.

A UN entry is one useful signal, not proof of application correctness, replicas, backups, latency objectives or full cluster health. Correlate authorized connection/read-write checks and operational signals. Load, UUID and ownership figures vary by environment. JMX/internode ports must remain private; enabling a CQL password alone is not complete production hardening.

No operations lab: no repair, forced compaction, decommission, join/leave, failure injection or multi-node deployment is required or claimed. Token ownership/replication is explained conceptually; the real dataset was tested on one physical node only.

title.en: Answered Practical Revision Tasks — Not a Theory Question Paper

h.en: Explain a Cassandra peer, coordinator, partition and replica without claiming the local lab is a three-node cluster.

body.en:
A peer can coordinate a request and communicate with the relevant replica nodes. Partitioning divides data subsets using partition-key placement; replication keeps additional copies according to the keyspace policy.

The diagram is conceptual. The actual reference used one authenticated node and RF 1, so four logical device/day partitions do not establish multi-machine placement, replicated failover or global throughput.

h.en: Prepare a compatible, private Cassandra/cqlsh setup and a real storage-verification journal.

body.en:
Identify OS/architecture and the selected release; install supported Java and matching cqlsh/Python; verify the official download checksum; configure private interfaces and authorized lab access; start the server; connect with a hidden password or protected credentials; record actual versions and an insert/read round-trip.

The tested reference was Debian 13 x86_64, Cassandra 5.0.9, cqlsh 6.2.0, Python 3.13.16 and Temurin 17.0.21+9. The factory role was disabled/rotated. Do not claim those steps are production hardening or use public default credentials.

h.en: Compare PRIMARY KEY (device_id,day,reading_at) with PRIMARY KEY ((device_id,day),reading_at).

body.en:
The first partitions on device_id and clusters by day then reading_at; all days of one device share that partition. The second partitions on the pair device_id/day and clusters only by reading_at; a new day creates another logical partition.

Both complete keys identify one row. Choose the layout from required reads and expected size/load. A partition is not a server, and a daily bucket is not automatically bounded safely for every write rate.

h.en: Design the sensor-history table and explain int, text, date and timestamp literals.

body.en:
Use device_id text, day date, reading_at timestamp, temperature_c double and status text with PRIMARY KEY ((device_id,day),reading_at) and descending time order.

int is a signed 32-bit integer; text uses single-quoted UTF-8 string values; date stores a calendar day; timestamp stores date/time with millisecond precision. Include an explicit zone such as Z, and do not confuse double-quoted identifiers with string values. Wrong-type and null primary keys are rejected.

h.en: Demonstrate Create/Alter/Drop keyspaces and tables, and state the safety/primary-key limitations.

body.en:
Create a new owned prefix-scoped keyspace with NetworkTopologyStrategy, the actual datacenter1 and RF 1 for this single-node lab. Select it; retain durable writes; create a typed table, add/write/drop a regular column, change a comment and drop the table/keyspace after verification.

Refuse pre-existing namespaces. ALTER is not arbitrary primary-key repartitioning; a key-layout change needs a new model/migration. Stop after unexpected setup failures rather than continuing into someone else’s data and a DROP footer.

h.en: Insert learner 1 again using only a new name. Contrast the observed CQL behaviour with a MongoDB duplicate _id insertion.

body.en:
The normal CQL INSERT upserts: learner 1 becomes Asha Patel while existing city Surat and marks 82 remain; the logical row count for that key is one. Omitted existing regular columns are not removed.

That is not a normal MongoDB insertOne duplicate-ID error or whole-document replacement. Conditional/LWT variants have separate semantics and costs; do not assume they are implicit.

h.en: Query ID 2, then IDs 1 and 3, then an absent ID, selecting only required columns.

body.en:
WHERE learner_id=2 returns Ravi/Bharuch; WHERE learner_id IN (1,3) returns the two known identities/names; WHERE learner_id=999 returns an empty result set.

SELECT column lists shape returned data, not storage or authorization. Do not infer global name/marks ordering from a multi-partition result. Large IN fan-out and unsupported regular-field predicates need deliberate design.

h.en: Derive latest two, earliest two and the [09:00,09:02) query for S01/day29.

body.en:
The partition contains 30.0 at 09:00, 31.0 at 09:01 and 32.0 at 09:02 UTC. Default descending time with LIMIT 2 returns 32.0 then 31.0. Allowed ORDER BY reading_at ASC LIMIT 2 returns 30.0 then 31.0.

The half-open interval includes 09:00 and 09:01, excludes 09:02 and follows the default descending order: 31.0 then 30.0. This is not an unrestricted SQL ORDER BY on any regular field.

h.en: Update Ravi’s city/marks and update previously absent learner 99. Explain the real results.

body.en:
SET city=Surat and marks=75 for ID 2 reads back Ravi/Surat/75. SET name=Jai and marks=68 for missing ID 99 creates that row with city null.

Normal UPDATE is an upsert and does not return matchedCount/modifiedCount. Use the correct complete row identity; do not use ordinary-int marks=marks+5 as a mechanical translation of MongoDB $inc.

h.en: Compare deleting a city cell, learner row, one sensor row and a device/day partition.

body.en:
DELETE city leaves Asha/82 with city null. Deleting ID 2 yields no learner row. Deleting the full S01/day29/09:02 key leaves two readings; deleting S02/day29 without a time removes that entire selected partition.

These scopes are different. Deletes use tombstones, so missing SELECT data is not immediate physical-erasure proof. No deletedCount is returned and no repair/compaction operation is required for this lesson.

h.en: Design device/day and status/day access paths and explain the 32.0 → 35.0 stale-copy experiment.

body.en:
Use readings_by_device_day for one device’s history and readings_by_status_day partitioned by status/day for a different lookup. Deliberate duplicated rows avoid a join or broad scan for these queries.

The base correction reads 35.0 while the second table still has 32.0. A separate explicit second write produces 35.0 there. There is no automatic foreign-key/cascade correction or implicit cross-table SQL transaction; applications must define retry/correction policies.

h.en: Explain the rejected temperature-only queries, the bounded ALLOW FILTERING example and the negative type/order/key tests.

body.en:
The unindexed temperature-only WHERE is rejected with InvalidRequest, even with LIMIT 1. After fixing S01/day29, ALLOW FILTERING explicitly scans its three known rows and returns 32.0/31.0.

It is not an index or performance promise. Wrong int literal, null primary key, regular-column ORDER BY and SET on a primary-key field are also rejected; malformed SELECT yields SyntaxException. The three valid learner rows remain unchanged.

h.en: Import sensors.csv with actual cqlsh and prove that distinct event keys and UTC times survived.

body.en:
Create the empty sensor table, run cqlsh COPY FROM with the explicit column list, HEADER, one worker, zero tolerated import/parse errors and DATETIMEFORMAT using %z for the Z suffix.

Verify eight stored rows against every CSV key/value/time, four logical partition values and latest S01/day29 time 09:02 with 32.0. A processed-row message is not enough: incorrect timestamp parsing or duplicate full keys can collapse rows through upserts. This is a synthetic snapshot, not live ingestion.

h.en: Calculate the per-partition feature summaries and explain their honest AI relevance.

body.en:
S01/day29 has 30+31+32 = 93 over three samples: mean 31, min 30, max 32. S02/day29 has mean 28.5; S01/day30 has mean 33.5; S03/day29 has mean 27.

These bounded real CQL aggregates can feed a report or later model. They do not train a classifier, guarantee real-time decisions, benchmark distributed throughput or justify unrestricted production full-table scans.

h.en: Interpret the actual UN observation and describe what is outside the health-awareness syllabus.

body.en:
nodetool status uses management/JMX. U/D are Up/Down; N/L/J/M are Normal/Leaving/Joining/Moving. The actual private reference showed one local UN node in datacenter1.

It is one useful observation, not proof of all application/backup/replica/latency guarantees. Keep management access private. No repair, decommission, join/leave, forced compaction, failure injection or multi-node deployment is required or claimed.

h.en: Prepare a Practical 4–6 acceptance checklist and explain why these tasks are not a theory paper.

body.en:
Record actual platform/versions, private authorized storage evidence, query-to-key reasoning, all DDL/CRUD/WHERE/ORDER BY/LIMIT outputs, expected errors and owned scratch cleanup. For the dataset verify every CSV row/time, four logical partitions and the bounded analytic calculations; record read-only health interpretation.

Keep credentials out of submissions and state single-node/synthetic limits. Official assessment is practical PA 20 + practical ESE 30 = 50 with zero theory ESE/PA. These answered revision tasks carry no invented official theory-paper marks.

title.en: Typed CQL Columns, Fixed UTC Timestamp and UUID

expl.en:
CQL tables have an explicit typed schema. int, text, timestamp, date, boolean, double and uuid are genuine stored types; strings use single quotes and the UUID literal is unquoted.

The runner displays timestamps in ISO UTC and date/UUID values as JSON strings. That display conversion does not change their CQL storage types. A fixed timestamp avoids machine-local timezone ambiguity.

title.en: Composite Partition Keys and Ordered Rows

expl.en:
Eight explicit seed records occupy four logical device/day partitions. PRIMARY KEY ((device_id,day),reading_at) uses both fields as the partition key; reading_at is the clustering column in descending order.

The same device on another day belongs to another partition. DISTINCT partition-key output is not a global lexical sort, and four logical partitions on this single physical node do not prove multi-node distribution.

A new primary key creates a new row; missing non-key values display as null. This is not whole-row replacement and does not return MongoDB-style inserted/modified counts.

There is no hidden extra seed for this example. Explicit DATETIMEFORMAT with %z preserves the UTC times; a processed-row message alone is not proof of distinct stored rows.

The runner captures COPY completion while omitting changing rates/timings from the published output; JSON rows are real server results. This small snapshot simulates time-stamped AI/IoT input, not a live stream, a trained model, an ETL benchmark or placement across multiple machines.

title.en: Foundations and Keys

q.en: What type of NoSQL database is Cassandra?

a.en: A distributed wide-column database with typed CQL tables organized into partitions and clustered rows.

q.en: Is wide-column the same as a columnar analytical warehouse?

a.en: No. Cassandra is designed around partition-oriented access and distributed storage; do not infer unrestricted analytical scans from the word column.

q.en: Give a suitable workload for the reference model.

a.en: A device/day sensor history with frequent timestamped writes and reads for one device over a bounded time range.

q.en: What does query-first design mean?

a.en: Write the required read patterns first, then choose partition/clustering keys and access tables that serve them predictably.

q.en: Is there one mandatory global write-primary?

a.en: No. Cassandra peers can coordinate requests; a coordinator is a per-request role, not a single cluster-wide primary.

q.en: Partitioning versus replication?

a.en: Partitioning divides logical data subsets; replication stores extra copies. Four partition keys do not imply four nodes or four replicas.

q.en: What is a keyspace?

a.en: A namespace for tables and related schema with options such as replication policy and durable writes.

q.en: What is a partition?

a.en: The rows sharing the complete partition-key value. A physical node may store many partitions.

q.en: What identifies one logical row?

a.en: The entire primary key: partition-key component(s) plus any clustering columns.

q.en: What does PRIMARY KEY ((a,b),c) mean?

a.en: a and b together form a composite partition key; c is the clustering column. Without the extra parentheses, a alone would be the partition key.

title.en: Setup and Typed Schema

q.en: What exact runtime was tested?

a.en: Cassandra 5.0.9, cqlsh 6.2.0, CQL 3.4.7, bundled Python driver 3.29.0, Python 3.13.16 and Temurin Java 17.0.21+9 on Debian 13 x86_64.

q.en: How many physical nodes were tested?

a.en: One private authenticated local node, with lab keyspaces using datacenter1 and RF 1. No multi-node availability or throughput test is claimed.

q.en: Why use matching cqlsh?

a.en: A client is generally guaranteed for its own Cassandra release; do not assume arbitrary old/new versions or Python interpreters are interchangeable.

q.en: Does cqlsh --version prove a stored write worked?

a.en: No. Connect, inspect actual server versions and verify an authorized insert/read round-trip as well.

q.en: What did SHOW VERSION report?

a.en: cqlsh 6.2.0, Cassandra 5.0.9, CQL spec 3.4.7 and native protocol v4. Protocol 4 is a selected wire-protocol version, not the Cassandra product version.

q.en: Why does the replication map use datacenter1?

a.en: That is the actual local datacenter name verified from system.local. An unrelated DC name is not a universal template.

q.en: Does RF 1 provide another node’s copy?

a.en: No. It is appropriate only for this one-node teaching reference and does not provide a replica for node loss.

q.en: Name required/basic CQL types.

a.en: int, text and timestamp; the typed example also stores date, boolean, double and uuid with their real CQL types.

q.en: Single quotes versus double quotes in CQL?

a.en: Single quotes delimit string values; double quotes delimit case-sensitive identifiers. Double an embedded apostrophe inside a string.

q.en: What does adding city text do to existing rows?

a.en: It adds a regular typed column; the previous row shows city null until it is written. It does not invent a default city or repartition data.

title.en: CRUD and Negative Cases

q.en: What happens on a normal INSERT of an existing full key?

a.en: It upserts supplied values for that logical row. In the demo Asha becomes Asha Patel while the omitted existing Surat/82 values remain.

q.en: Is normal INSERT a whole-row replacement?

a.en: No. It writes supplied values; omitted existing columns are not removed merely because they are absent from the INSERT list.

q.en: What happens on a normal UPDATE of missing learner 99?

a.en: It creates Jai/68 with city null. Basic UPDATE does not require the row to have existed.

q.en: Are matchedCount and modifiedCount returned by basic CQL updates?

a.en: No. Those are MongoDB-style result fields, not the normal CQL result. Handle errors and inspect the intended stored state.

q.en: Can marks=marks+5 update an ordinary int?

a.en: Not as ordinary CQL int arithmetic. Counter columns and collection operations have separate rules; do not translate MongoDB $inc mechanically.

q.en: What does deleting just city leave for learner 1?

a.en: The row still has Asha and marks 82, while city reads as null.

q.en: What key deletes one sensor reading?

a.en: The complete device_id/day/reading_at row identity. Supplying just device/day intentionally targets that entire partition.

q.en: What is a tombstone?

a.en: A logical deletion marker. A missing read result does not prove immediate physical byte erasure from disk.

q.en: Can SET change a primary-key field into another ID?

a.en: No. The real server rejects that mutation. A key is row identity; changing identity/model needs deliberate new data and cleanup.

q.en: How are null and wrong-type primary keys handled?

a.en: The shown null key and quoted one-as-int are rejected with real InvalidRequest exceptions; no extra valid row is inserted.

title.en: Queries and Modeling

q.en: What does a missing-key SELECT return?

a.en: An empty result set, not a new row and not a MongoDB findOne-style null value.

q.en: What do the latest-two and earliest-two queries return?

a.en: For S01/day29, descending latest values are 32.0 then 31.0; allowed ascending reverse order gives 30.0 then 31.0.

q.en: What does [09:00,09:02) include here?

a.en: 09:00 and 09:01, but not 09:02. The declared descending clustering order returns 31.0 then 30.0.

q.en: Can ORDER BY sort any regular column globally?

a.en: No. The shown ORDER BY uses a clustering column with required partition restrictions. ORDER BY marks in the learner table is rejected.

q.en: Does LIMIT 1 legalize the temperature-only WHERE?

a.en: No. That demonstrated unindexed non-key query remains invalid. LIMIT restricts returned rows; it does not create the access path.

q.en: What does ALLOW FILTERING mean in this fixture?

a.en: It explicitly permits residual filtering after selecting the known three-row partition. It is not an index or a guarantee of scalable performance.

q.en: Why use a status/day table as well as a device/day table?

a.en: They serve different read patterns without a join or broad scan; the intentional duplication requires coordinated correction/deletion policies.

q.en: What did the denormalization correction demonstrate?

a.en: The base reading changed from 32.0 to 35.0 while the second table stayed at 32.0 until a separate explicit write updated it. There is no automatic cross-table correction.

title.en: Dataset and Analytical Features

q.en: How many sensor rows and logical partitions are in sensors.csv?

a.en: Eight synthetic rows in four device/day partitions: S01/day29 has 3, S02/day29 has 2, S01/day30 has 2 and S03/day29 has 1.

q.en: Is COPY FROM native CQL?

a.en: No. It is a cqlsh special command. The reference runner delegates it to real matching cqlsh rather than pretending a driver supports it.

q.en: Why use DATETIMEFORMAT with %z?

a.en: To parse the CSV’s explicit UTC Z suffix correctly. Wrong parsing or duplicate full keys can collapse distinct records into upserts.

q.en: Is eight processed/imported rows enough verification?

a.en: No. Verify eight distinct stored rows, all full keys/values/times, four logical partition keys and the correct latest UTC reading.

q.en: What is the S01/day29 aggregate?

a.en: Three samples, sum 93.0, mean 31.0, minimum 30.0 and maximum 32.0.

q.en: What are the other per-partition means?

a.en: S02/day29 is 28.5, S01/day30 is 33.5 and S03/day29 is 27.0.

q.en: Is the CSV example a live stream or trained AI system?

a.en: No. It is a reproducible synthetic snapshot with real database import and simple feature/report calculations, not live hardware, model training or a throughput benchmark.

q.en: Why are time buckets not automatically safe at every rate?

a.en: Partition size and hotness depend on writes per time unit, row size and access load. A daily bucket may need to be smaller or differently designed for a much faster stream.

title.en: Health, Safety and Evidence

q.en: What does nodetool status use?

a.en: Management/JMX, not a CQL statement inside cqlsh. Management access must be private and authorized.

q.en: What do UN and DN mean?

a.en: U/D indicate Up/Down; N indicates Normal. The actual reference observed one local UN node. Other state letters include L/J/M for Leaving/Joining/Moving.

q.en: Does UN prove every application and availability guarantee?

a.en: No. It is one signal; correlate application reads/writes and operational evidence. It does not prove backups, multiple replicas or latency objectives.

q.en: Were repair, decommission or failure injection tested?

a.en: No. The syllabus asks for nodetool/cluster-health awareness only. The only management observation was read-only status.

q.en: How does the guarded runner protect existing keyspaces?

a.en: It validates the dedicated prefix, refuses an existing namespace, records ownership only after CREATE succeeds and finally drops only that captured newly owned keyspace.

q.en: What assessment and completion boundary should the journal state?

a.en: Practical PA 20 + ESE 30 = 50 with no theory ESE/PA. Record Practicals 4–6 and real single-node evidence; no official theory paper, multi-node proof or external hosting is claimed.
